Stated Claim / Post Context:
Nassau County has a Flock Safety camera every 9.5 miles, residents among one of America’s most surveilled: Data

Flock Safety is a controversial brand of AI-powered cameras that scan and store info on every car that drives past, including license plates and distinct features like dents and bumper stickers.

Actual Article Body:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.

See more of our coverage in your search results.

Big Brother’s watching the island.

Nassau County drivers pass a Flock Safety camera roughly every 9.5 miles, making its residents some of the most heavily surveilled and tracked in the nation, according to independent data.

The county now has more than 330 Flock Safety cameras publicly mapped on over 3,200 miles of road, placing Nassau within the top 100 counties in the country for cameras per mile, according to open-source data compiled by DeFlock, an activist group tracking the company’s surveillance and expansion.

That works out to roughly 105 Flock Safety cameras for every 1,000 miles of road — or one camera installed less than every 10 miles, according to the data.

This places Nassau County residents within the top 3% of the most closely watched drivers in America, as the county’s massive Flock camera density topped more than 3,100 other counties nationwide, the data detailed.

Flock Safety is a controversial brand of AI-powered cameras that scan and store info on every car that drives past, including license plates and distinct features like dents and bumper stickers.

That data is then searchable to cops around the country and able to be used to track a vehicle’s movements.

Neighboring Suffolk County, meanwhile, has a few hundred cameras mapped across roughly 7,100 miles of road, or about one every 33 miles, ranking it within the top 500 in the nation.

However, it appears not all of the Flock Safety cameras in Suffolk County have been mapped by the activist site, leaving an unclear amount still unaccounted for, according to an analysis by The Post.

The gap comes as Suffolk officials are seemingly looking to catch up — but just delayed a $4 million deal with Flock Safety for its controversial “Raven” listening system earlier this month. The county is continuing to explore a possible separate deal for more county-owned cameras with the brand.

Last year, Nassau County inked its own, $1 million deal with Flock Safety to purchase an undisclosed amount of cameras from the controversial brand, according to a recording of a November 2025 legislature meeting.

Last week, The Post reported that Long Island cops ran almost 3,000 manual searches in Flock’s database in just the month of June.

In total, there are about 600 Flock cameras installed over 100 miles between the Queens border and Montauk, with thousands more throughout the five boroughs, according to the data.

Flock’s surveillance system, which has quietly become law enforcement’s go-to surveillance tool around the country, has also become a major source of controversy — prompting nationwide protests, the birth of anti-Flock activist organizations, and instances of vigilante vandalism.

Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman recently told The Post that he believes Flock “is an important tool in law enforcement,” but said he would “never allow that tool to be used in an improper way.”

“We have put in place strict guidelines to protect privacy and eliminate any potential for abuse, using information gathered by Flock Cameras,” he said.

More than 60 cops nationwide have been arrested for misusing Flock data, with 18 in Georgia this summer alone, including a police supervisor who used the camera system to track her boyfriend, reports said.

A slew of bills have also been introduced to regulate the technology on both sides of the aisle, with lefty Sen. Bernie Sanders proposing to ban the technology outright while libertarian Rep. Thomas Massie’s bill would strip federal funding from local departments that deploy it.

Both Nassau and Suffolk Counties, along with multiple local towns, cities, and villages within them who also have deals with Flock Safety, would lose federal funding under Massie’s bill if passed.
